title: Azariah's Word and Asa's Covenant Renewal
summary: After the victory over Zerah, the prophet Azariah son of Oded meets Asa with a promise and a warning: the LORD is with those who are with him, and he will be found by those who seek him. Encouraged, Asa removes idols throughout his territory, repairs the altar, and gathers Judah, Benjamin, and many northerners in Jerusalem, where they sacrifice and swear a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul. Asa even removes his grandmother Maacah as queen mother because of her Asherah pole.
story: Chapter 14 showed Asa seeking God in peace and relying on him in war. Here a prophet interprets that success and turns it into a lasting commitment. Victory could have made Asa proud, as strength made Rehoboam careless (12:1), but Azariah's word leads him deeper into reform. The chapter is the high point of Asa's reign and one of several covenant renewals in Chronicles, anticipating the later ones under Jehoiada (chapter 23), Hezekiah (chapter 29), and Josiah (chapter 34). The next chapter will show how, many years later, Asa loses his way.
historical:
Azariah son of Oded appears only here, one of several prophets in Chronicles who are not mentioned in Kings. His survey of a time when Israel was without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without the law (verses 3 to 6) sounds most like the period of the judges, when there was disorder and repeated turning to God in distress, though some interpreters think he is describing the recent condition of the northern kingdom, or speaking in terms that fit any time of apostasy. The gathering in Jerusalem took place in Asa's fifteenth year, about 896 BC on the usual chronology.

The northerners from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who had settled in Judah continue the movement begun in chapter 11, where the faithful from the north came south to worship. Simeon's territory lay within Judah's in the south (Joshua 19:1-9), so its mention with northern tribes is a puzzle; it may reflect Simeonites who had become associated with the north, or the Chronicler's concern to show representatives of all Israel gathering. Asa's removal of Maacah is also recorded in 1 Kings 15:13, which calls her Asa's mother; the Hebrew word can mean grandmother or ancestress, and she was Abijah's mother (11:20-22), so the BSB translates it as grandmother.
cultural:
The queen mother held an official position at the court of Judah, with real influence, and the books of Kings name the mother of almost every king of Judah. Deposing Maacah was a public act that cost Asa politically and within his family. The Asherah pole she made is described with a rare word meaning something horrifying or shocking, which suggests an especially offensive image. Burning it in the Kidron Valley, the ravine east of Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives, became the customary way kings of Judah disposed of idols (compare 29:16 and 30:14).

The covenant ceremony follows ancient practice: an assembly, sacrifices, a sworn oath before God, and public celebration with trumpets and rams' horns (the shofar). The third month of the year, when the gathering took place, was the time of the Feast of Weeks, a harvest festival, and some interpreters see a deliberate link between the festival and the oath. The sacrifices came from the plunder of the war in chapter 14, so the spoil of victory was given back to God.
literary: Azariah's short sermon (verses 2 to 7) is built on conditional statements: the LORD is with you when you are with him; if you seek him he will be found, but if you forsake him he will forsake you. The rest of the chapter shows the conditions fulfilled on the positive side. The phrase "He was found by them" appears in the history lesson of verse 4 and again in verse 15, where it describes Judah's own experience, so the sermon's promise comes true within the chapter. The words seek, heart, and rest tie the covenant scene together, and rest on every side in verse 15 echoes 14:7. The closing notices (verses 16 to 19) show the reform reaching even the royal family and the temple treasury.

outline.t: Azariah's prophecy: seek the LORD and he will be found
Asa removes idols, repairs the altar, and gathers the people
The covenant to seek the LORD with all heart and soul
Maacah removed, gifts brought to the temple, and years of peace

doctrines.note: The people bind themselves by oath to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul, echoing the language of Deuteronomy 6:5. Covenant renewal is how Israel recommitted to the relationship God had already established with them.
The Spirit of God comes upon Azariah to speak, as the Spirit often comes upon prophets in the Old Testament. The Spirit's work here is to bring God's word at the right moment.

Azariah's history lesson shows a pattern: in distress Israel turned to the LORD and sought him, and he was found. Returning to God is always possible, and he is not hidden from those who genuinely look for him.

words.note: Matsa, to find, or in the passive, to be found. God allowing himself to be found by those who seek him is the promise of the chapter, stated in verse 2 and fulfilled in verse 15. It echoes Deuteronomy 4:29 and anticipates Jeremiah 29:13-14.

Darash, to seek. The verb dominates Asa's story. Here it becomes the content of a covenant: to seek the LORD with all heart and soul. In Chronicles this is the essence of faithfulness, and failure to seek becomes the charge against unfaithful kings.

Shevu'ah, oath. A solemn sworn promise before God. Verse 15 says the people rejoiced over the oath because they had sworn it with all their heart, which presents the commitment as joyful rather than grudging.
Miphletset, something horrifying or shocking, used only in this account and its parallel in 1 Kings 15:13. It describes Maacah's Asherah image and marks it as especially abhorrent.

christ: Azariah's promise that God will be found by those who seek him runs through the Bible to Jesus' words, seek and you will find (Matthew 7:7), and to the claim of the New Testament that God has made himself found in the person of his Son (John 14:9). The covenant sworn in Jerusalem, with its call to love God with all the heart and soul, is the command Jesus named as the greatest (Mark 12:29-30). The prophets knew that Israel's covenant renewals did not last, and they looked for a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), which the New Testament says Christ established by his blood (Luke 22:20). The connection is thematic, drawn from the covenant pattern rather than from anything predictive in the chapter.

hard.q: Verse 13 says that anyone who would not seek the LORD should be put to death. How should this be understood?
hard.a: The penalty follows the law of Deuteronomy, which required death for those in Israel who led others into, or practiced, the worship of other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6-10, 17:2-7). In ancient Israel the covenant with God was also the nation's constitution, so apostasy was treated as treason against the covenant community. Many interpreters also note that the clause functions as the curse sanction of the oath, the penalty the swearers invoked on themselves, rather than a record of executions actually carried out. Christians have generally held that this civil enforcement of worship belonged to Israel as a nation under the old covenant and is not a pattern for the church, which Jesus did not authorize to wield the sword (Matthew 26:52; John 18:36). The history of Christians coercing belief is one the church has had to repent of. Readers still feel the severity of the verse, and it shows how seriously Israel understood its covenant with God.

questions: Azariah said, “The LORD is with you when you are with Him.” How does that statement both comfort and challenge you?
Asa removed his own grandmother from power because of her idol. When has faithfulness to God cost you something with people close to you?
The people rejoiced over their oath because they made it with all their heart. What makes the difference between commitment that feels like a burden and commitment that brings joy?
